steps: Unpack & inspect

Inspect the stove and parts for transit damage; the pack list is the stove, owner's manual and removable bypass handle. Remove the packaging material in the flue collar and above the baffle before installing the chimney.

Report damaged or missing parts to the Hearthstone dealer right away.

The label is attached by a cable to the bottom of the stove; don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning, store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
Site the stove
Freestanding room heater only; not to be installed in any factory-built fireplace. Prefer a main living area and check clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase before connecting.

Keep it out of traffic flow, doors and hallways, and near an existing chimney if possible. Never install in or near storage of gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or other flammable liquids. Avoid basements, confined spaces and poorly insulated areas.
Floor protection
Combustible floors need a non-combustible floor protector: 40in x 34in minimum (US), 49 1/2in x 41in (Canada). No insulated hearth pad or R-value is required; check LVP/LVT flooring limits.

Example protector: a hearth with a continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass or another non-combustible facing, under the stove and extending beyond it (layout in Figure 3). Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit; extra shielding may be needed.
Clearances to combustibles

Set wall and corner clearances from the Figure 4 table for the connector (single or double wall) and rear heat shield (kit #90-68210). Reduce clearances only with the Hearthstone shield, listed close-clearance pipe or NFPA 211 protection.

The table's columns A–F are defined only in the drawing on p. 10; connector clearances are in Figure 5 on p. 11. Values shown are typical for Simpson Dura-Vent DVL; check the listing of the pipe you use.
Outside air (optional kit)
Kit #90-53220 connects the stove's air intake to a minimum 3" (76 mm) duct (4" adaptor kit #90-53308). Terminate no higher than the intake, screened with ¼" x ¼" mesh and a rain/wind proof hood.

The kit attaches to the underside of the stove; follow the kit's instructions. The IRC does not allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance. Place the termination where snow or leaves can't block it. Duct, termination, mesh and hood are not supplied.

Required in all mobile home installations. Canada: install a damper allowing 100% closure and attach the stove to the floor with the shipping clips.
Chimney connector

6" 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel (no aluminum or galvanized), crimped end toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint (#10 x 1/2" into the flue collar holes). Keep it short and straight; horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

The connector cannot pass through a floor or ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or similar concealed space. Through a combustible wall, use a wall thimble or pass-through per NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA - B365. Pass-through constructions listed on p. 12:

  • A: minimum 3.5in thick brick framed into the wall, minimum 12in brick separation from clay liner to combustibles.
  • B: listed factory-built chimney length, same inside diameter, 1in or more insulation, minimum 9in air space.
  • C: minimum 24 gauge connector with a ventilated 24 gauge thimble (two 1in air channels), minimum 6in of glass fiber insulation.
  • D: listed factory-built chimney length 2in larger in diameter, 1in or more insulation, minimum 2in air space, minimum 12in long.

Double-wall connector reduces clearances with a listed Type HT or masonry chimney (e.g. Simpson Dura Vent DVL, Metalbestos DS). Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct.
Draft requirement
Check the draft at installation; install a stovepipe damper for drafts above -0.1" WC. The manual's lower limit differs by page: -0.08" WC on p. 14, -0.06" WC on p. 16.

Tall chimneys can over-draft; some installations need more than one damper.

Note: p. 14 gives the required draft as -0.08" to -0.1" WC; p. 16 gives -0.06" to -0.1" WC.
Note: p. 14 gives the minimum draft for a rear exit as -0.08" WC; p. 15 gives -0.06" WC.
Rear flue exit (if used)
Ships in the vertical (top) configuration. To exit the rear, swap the flue collar and flue plate and trim the rear heat shield for the pipe.

1. With a 5/32" hex key, remove the two screws inside the flue collar and lift it off the top.
  2. Remove the rear heat shield, if equipped (loosen four screws, lift off).
  3. With the 5/32" hex key, remove the flue plate from the back (two screws).
  4. Fit the flue collar on the back and the flue plate on top, 2 screws each. Keep the ¼" gasket in both channels.
  5. Cut the section out of the rear heat shield with metal snips so the pipe passes through.
  6. Re-install the rear heat shield.

Don't use the rear exit without sufficient draft.

Note: p. 15 gives the minimum chimney height for a rear exit as 15'; p. 16 recommends 19 feet off the floor (16 feet 5 3/4 inches from the top of the stove).
Connect to the chimney

Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner; 6" (152 mm) inside diameter for new installs, an existing 8" (203 mm) flue with a reducer. Top at least 3 feet above the roof opening and 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet.

Chimney size: not less than the flue collar, not more than three times its cross-sectional area. Have a masonry chimney professionally examined and repaired first; its cleanout door must seal tightly. Interior chimney: 2" (51 mm) clearance to combustibles, fire stops at floors and ceilings. Exterior chimney: 1" (25 mm). With prefabricated chimney, buy the pass-through, tee, fire-stops, shield, flashing and cap from the same manufacturer. A cleanout tee is recommended.
Mobile home (US only)
Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD); not approved for mobile homes in Canada. Outside air kit required, stove attached to the floor with the shipping clips, never in a sleeping room.

• Mobile Home Chimney & Connector Kit to UL103: stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove, at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes and 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet; secured to the ceiling support box.
  • Roof terminations removable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools.
  • Spark arrester openings must stop a ½" sphere and pass a 3/8" sphere.
  • A chimney leaving other than through the roof, 7 feet or less above ground, needs a guard up to 7 feet.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof; remove the chimney when the home is moved.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → open the air control fully a minute before opening the door; open the bypass first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window
Blocked, oversized, undersized or short chimney → clear it, reline, add a draft inducer or lengthen it
Air leaking into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed in the active range, or catalysts not working → close it; inspect, brush or replace the catalysts
Wet wood, or another appliance on the flue → seasoned dry cordwood; disconnect other appliances

panels.title: Back-puffing
items: Operating technique → air fully open a minute before opening the door and a few minutes after reloading; bypass open first
Extra low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty the ash pan more often; avoid poor-quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets
Air leaking around the glass gasket → replace the gasket
Excessive draft → operate at low burn; correct draft over 0.1 wc with stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long or oversized chimney → shorten it or add damper(s); reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Catalyst problems
items: Fly ash build-up (light-off not kept, bypass closed too soon, char-heavy materials) → brush the cold combustor or vacuum lightly
Plugging or masking with soot/creosote (wet or pitchy wood, engaged before light-off) → hot fire, then run high for one hour with catalysts in the upper range
Warping or bowing (too hot for long periods) → lower the air setting to keep catalysts in range

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Use this for everyday fires once the stove is broken in.

  1. Move the bypass handle to Bypass.
  2. Open the front door. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Stand about 10 pieces of kindling over it in a tee-pee, each about 1/2" in diameter and 10" to 16" long.
  3. Open the primary air control fully by pulling the lever all the way out.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment, until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull.
  5. Close the door and let the fire burn.
  6. Once the kindling is burning, open the door and add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass.
  7. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst thermometer shows the active range, move the bypass handle to Engage.
  8. Run the stove on high for about 20 minutes. This keeps the catalysts active and burns residue off the glass.
  9. Then set the burn rate you want with the primary air control.
Build the fire right on the firebox floor, toward the center. Don't use a grate. Keep the front door closed while the stove is in use.

breakin.title: Breaking in your stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned slowly. Firing a new stove too hot can crack the stone or damage other parts. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season after that, this way:

  1. Move the bypass handle to Bypass.
  2. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Lay about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" in diameter, 10" to 16" long) crisscross over it.
  3. Open the primary air control fully. Light the paper and leave the door slightly open for a moment, until the kindling catches.
  4. Close the door. Keep a steady, low fire: the stove should feel warm, not hot. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once the stove is warm, push the air control fully in and let the fire die out. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

What's normal

The first fires give off some smoke and fumes as the paint and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. A dark liquid may seep onto the hearth early on; set aluminum foil around each leg to catch it. Cool break-in fires can dirty the glass and build creosote fast, so look over the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is done.

bypass.title: Bypass handle & catalyst thermometer
bypass.html:
Your Mansfield burns off smoke in a catalytic combustor. The bypass handle sends smoke around the catalysts (Bypass, handle open) or through them (Engage, handle closed). The catalyst thermometer tells you which to use.

InactiveBypass, until the stove heats up
Catalyst ActiveEngage
Too HotKeep the door closed, close the air control fully, move the handle to Bypass, and let it cool back into Catalyst Active
  • Use Bypass when you start a fire and every time you open the door to load.
  • Switch to Engage once the catalysts are hot (they become active around 500 °F), and leave it there while the stove burns in the active range.

Once active, the burning smoke keeps the catalysts hot as long as there's fuel, and you should see little to no smoke from the chimney. The stove typically runs at 450 °F to 1200 °F flue gas temperature.

In Canada, the bypass handle must use the supplied removable adapter. Store the handle in its holder on the bottom heat shield when you're not using it.

burn.title: Burn rate & reloading
burn.html:
The primary air control lever is under the ash lip. Pull it toward you for a faster, hotter fire; push it toward the stove for a slower one. By design it never closes completely.

LowLever all the way in
Medium-lowFrom low, pull it out a little less than 1/4". The typical setting, and best if you'll be away.
Medium-highFrom low, pull it out a little less than 3/8"
HighLever all the way out

Long stretches on low build creosote. Run on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.

Reloading

  1. Move the bypass handle to Bypass.
  2. Open the door a crack, pause, then open it fully.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. Leave a small valley in the coals behind the lower primary air opening.
  4. If the fire was cool or down to charcoal, run it medium to high for about 10 minutes so the catalysts reach about 500 °F. Then move the handle to Engage.
Never over-fire the stove. Over-firing damages the stove and voids the warranty. Signs: warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or pipe, a discolored stovepipe. If you suspect over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). The stove isn't designed for any other fuel.

  • Dry wood matters most. Split, stack and air-dry green wood for a year. Seasoned firewood is typically at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Stack it right. Keep it off the ground on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Hardwood or softwood? Softwoods burn hotter and faster; hardwoods burn longer and make better coals. The manual ranks common species by heat content.
  • Don't store firewood inside the stove's clearances, and don't load ice-covered wood into a burning stove.
Never burn garbage or trash, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), plastic or asbestos, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), cardboard, plywood, particleboard or compressed wood, painted, treated or kiln-dried wood, unseasoned or green wood, railroad ties, construction or demolition debris, asphalt products, waste petroleum products, solvents, paints or paint thinners, manure or animal remains, driftwood or other material previously saturated with salt water, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or flammable fluids. Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or other flammable fluids to start or invigorate a fire. They will cause dangerous burning conditions in the stove. Keep all such materials away from the stove. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Anything other than natural firewood isn't safe to use as fuel; unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide, which could result in personal injury or death. Some of these also damage the catalysts.

Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, or sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox if you like.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and shovel out only the finer ash. Don't let ash build up at the door opening: it can spill out or pack into the gasket channel.
  3. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Put nothing else in it, and don't pour water in.
  4. Close the lid and take the container outdoors right away. Set it on a noncombustible surface away from buildings, combustibles, fuels and vehicles.
  5. Keep the lid on until every coal is completely cool.
Coals in ash can stay hot for several days. Never use wooden or plastic containers, trash cans or bags, and never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.

With the optional ash pan

Open the ash pan door and pull the handle out to open the grate; sift the ash through into the pan, then close the grate. Push the pan in hard before you lift it out. Only run the stove with the pan in and the ash door closed.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The door glass is a tough ceramic made for wood stoves. Clean it only when the stove is cool, never while it's hot or burning.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the inside of the glass in circles.
  2. When the deposits are gone, finish with window cleaner or a stove-glass cleaner. Use the same on the outside.
  3. Wipe it off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive. Scratches weaken the glass.

Glass that's always dirty

That means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet, which also raises the creosote risk. A good hot fire cleans it.

Broken or chipped glass

Don't run the stove with cracked or broken glass, and don't slam the door. Replace it right away with Hearthstone's glass kit (90-58215) from your dealer.

Note: p. 29 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; p. 30 says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace the glass yourself.

care.title: Upkeep checklist
care.html:
Every week

  • Empty the ashes, sooner if the firebox is full.

Every other month

  • Look over the stovepipe and chimney for creosote, the tar that builds up in a cool chimney and can catch fire. Until experience shows you how often you need to clean to be safe, check for creosote build-up every day.
  • Do the dollar-bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing. Adjust the latch or replace the gasket.
  • Check the face of the catalytic combustor for fly ash and soot, and brush it off with a soft-bristled brush. Look at it at least 3 times each heating season.

End of every season

  • Take down and clean the stovepipe; replace pieces that show rust or wear.
  • Inspect and, if needed, clean the chimney. Clean out the inside of the stove and check the combustor.
  • Replace door gasket that's worn, frayed, cracked or very hard. Plan on every two to three seasons.
If more than 1/4" of creosote builds up, have it removed; a certified chimney sweep is recommended. Have the whole system professionally inspected before each heating season.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. If the fire is threatening, leave and call the fire department right away. If not:
  2. Close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass damper.
  5. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. The heat can turn it to steam instantly and cause serious injury.

When the chimney fire is out, leave the air control and bypass handle closed and let the stove fire die out completely. Check the stove, stovepipe and chimney for damage, and fix any before you use the stove again.

Every day

  • Keep furniture, drapes and other combustibles at least 36" from the stove.
  • Keep children and pets away while it's burning.
  • Install smoke and CO detectors throughout the home, and keep an "A B C" fire extinguisher handy.
  • Keep the front door closed while it's burning, except to start and load it.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's limited warranty covers defects for the original purchaser only, on a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative. It can't be transferred and starts on the date of the original invoice. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Enamel finish (peeling or fading); glass; accessories1 year

Hearthstone pays warranty labor in the first year only if a dealer installed the stove, and pays parts shipping for the first 90 days. Other parts are in the warranty table.

Catalysts

The catalytic combustors are warranted by their maker, Applied Ceramics: free replacement if one stops working within two years, then prorated prices ($130.00 in year 3 up to $160.00 in year 6).

Not covered

  • Over-firing, the wrong fuel, or not following the manual
  • Normal wear on paint, gaskets, baffles, refractory, ash grates and glass
  • Surface and hairline cracks in the stone, expansion noises and odors

Claims go through your dealer. Registering at hearthstonestoves.com isn't required for coverage.
